tagline: River crossings and maritime villages along the Delaware Bay’s marsh shore
intro: The Bayshore Heritage Byway follows Delaware Bay from Mannington Township to Cape May Point State Park, moving inland between stretches of shoreline. River crossings, rolling farmland and historic villages give the drive its changing shape; the bay’s shores are largely wetland, salt marsh and mud flat. NJDOT lists a 122-mile main route, or 142 miles including spurs, and identifies nature and history as its defining qualities. It is also a National Scenic Byway. NJDOT links the route’s communities to the bay’s natural resources and the resting and feeding grounds used by migrating birds.

These roads connect communities whose work depended on the bay: fishing, oyster processing, shipbuilding and salt hay farming. Near Newport, coastal dirt roads once carried salt hay harvested for livestock bedding, fodder and garden mulch. At the Maurice River, East Point’s lighthouse was built in 1849; Bivalve’s oyster packing buildings followed in the 1870s.

Head south from Mannington through Salem to Greenwich, then inland to cross the Cohansey at Bridgeton. Continue through Fairton and Newport toward Port Norris, where a spur reaches Bivalve. Cross the Maurice River and take the East Point Lighthouse spur from Heislerville before continuing toward Cape May. The drive ends at Cape May Point State Park, with its birding platforms and boardwalk trail.

moments.title: Greenwich
moments.text: Tea bound for Philadelphia ended up in a Greenwich cellar, then in a fire. The Greyhound’s captain diverted his cargo to avoid confrontation in Philadelphia, but residents learned where it was stored. On December 22, 1774, colonists broke into the cellar, removed the tea and burned it. The Cumberland County Historical Society erected a monument to the event in 1908. The town’s historic district extends along both sides of Ye Greate Street, beside the tidal Cohansey River. The memorial stands at Main Street and Market Square, giving the episode a specific place in the present town.

moments.title: East Point Light
moments.text: East Point Light stands at the mouth of the Maurice River on Delaware Bay. Built in 1849, it was known as the Maurice River Light until 1913. The light went inactive in 1941, and a fire nearly destroyed it in 1971. The Coast Guard reinstated the light in 1980; exterior restoration followed in 1999, with a full restoration completed in 2017. The lighthouse serves as an active navigational aid under the stewardship of the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection. Its 1995 National Register listing recognizes the lighthouse’s significance in engineering, maritime history and transportation.

moments.title: Cape May Point State Park
moments.text: Southbound migrating birds find food and cover at Cape May Point while waiting for favorable winds across Delaware Bay. In 1935, the National Audubon Society leased twenty-five acres here for the Witmer Stone Wild Life Sanctuary. A wartime magnesite factory damaged its plants and wildlife, and the sanctuary was abandoned in 1959. Each fall, a hawk watch counts migrating birds of prey over several months. The park’s half-mile Red Trail is a boardwalk with observation platforms. The hawk platform, trails and beach provide different viewing places for raptors, songbirds and shorebirds. Trails and beach connect to the neighboring South Cape May Meadows.
